summary: Our proposed solution is an AI-powered astronaut healthcare monitoring system designed to continuously track and protect astronauts' physical and mental health during space missions. The system uses wearable sensors to collect real-time health data, including heart rate, blood oxygen levels, body temperature, sleep patterns, and stress indicators. An onboard AI model analyses this data to detect abnormalities, predict potential health complications, and provide early warnings. It also features an intelligent medical assistant that helps astronauts assess symptoms, receive preliminary medical guidance, and access suitable treatment instructions without relying on immediate communication with Earth. By maintaining individual health records and adapting recommendations to each astronaut's medical history, the system provides personalised healthcare. This solution aims to reduce medical risks, enable early intervention, and make long-duration space missions safer through continuous monitoring and autonomous medical assistance.
details: PushingFurther is an AI-powered healthcare monitoring system built to protect astronauts' physical and mental health on long-duration space missions. As missions move beyond low Earth orbit, communication delays and blackouts make real-time medical support from Earth unreliable, while radiation, microgravity and isolation put constant strain on the body and mind. Our system closes this gap by keeping a capable health guardian on board. Wearable sensors continuously collect heart rate, blood oxygen, body temperature, sleep patterns and stress indicators such as heart rate variability. This data flows into a lightweight edge pipeline that filters noise, normalises readings and stores them locally for each astronaut. An onboard AI engine then learns every astronaut's personal baseline, because "normal" differs from person to person. Anomaly detection models, such as an autoencoder and Isolation Forest, flag deviations in real time, while a time-series model forecasts risks like fatigue, dehydration, infection or cardiac stress hours before they become emergencies. Results appear as simple green, amber and red alerts on a crew dashboard. The system also includes an intelligent medical assistant. An astronaut can describe symptoms by voice or text, and the assistant combines them with live vitals and the astronaut's health record. It uses an offline language model grounded in space-medicine protocols to give preliminary assessments and step-by-step treatment guidance using the supplies in the onboard medical kit. Serious or uncertain cases are escalated to a flight surgeon on Earth with a full summary, so critical decisions always stay with a human doctor. Because everything runs offline on the spacecraft's own computer, the system keeps working without contact with Earth. Personalised records mean recommendations adapt to each crew member's history. Together, these features reduce medical risk, enable early intervention and make long-duration missions safer.
